label: lem:standard
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:standard}
Let $f\in S$ be reduced.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)},leftmargin=2em]
\item \textup{(Saito's criterion \cite{Saito})} Elements $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_N\in\operatorname{Der}(-\log f)$ form a basis if and only if $\det(\theta_i(y_j))=c\cdot f$ with $c$ a unit. For arbitrary $\theta_i\in\operatorname{Der}(-\log f)$ one always has $\det(\theta_i(y_j))\in fS$.
\item If $f$ is homogeneous and $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_N\in\operatorname{Der}(-\log f)$ are homogeneous with $\sum_i\deg\theta_i=\deg f$ \textup{(}in the convention above\textup{)} and $\det(\theta_i(y_j))\neq0$, then they form a basis. If $V(f)$ is free, the degrees of any homogeneous basis add up to $\deg f$.
\item The set of points where $V(f)$ is not free is Zariski closed. If $f$ is homogeneous, $V(f)$ is free everywhere if and only if it is free at $0$, if and only if the graded module $\operatorname{Der}(-\log f)$ is free.
\item If $\alpha\colon(\mathbb{C}^N,p)\to(\mathbb{C}^{N-k},p')\times(\mathbb{C}^k,0)$ is a local analytic isomorphism taking $V(f)$ to $V(f')\times\mathbb{C}^k$, then $\operatorname{Der}(-\log f)_p\cong\operatorname{Der}(-\log f')_{p'}\oplus\mathcal O^k$. In particular, $V(f)$ is free at $p$ if and only if $V(f')$ is free at $p'$.
\item If $\operatorname{Der}(-\log f)$ is generated by $g$ elements with presentation matrix $P$, then the stalk at $p$ is minimally generated by $g-\operatorname{rk} P(p)$ elements. Here $P(p)$ is the scalar matrix obtained by evaluating $P$ at $p$. In particular, $V(f)$ is not free at $p$ if and only if $\operatorname{rk} P(p)<g-N$.
\item Formation of $\operatorname{Der}(-\log f)$ commutes with flat base change. In particular, if $f$ has rational coefficients, computations over $\mathbb{Q}$ give the answer over $\mathbb{C}$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Item (a) is \cite[(1.8)]{Saito}. The second assertion holds because at a smooth point of $V(f)$ all $\theta_i$ are tangent to $V(f)$, so the determinant vanishes on $V(f)$, and $f$ is reduced. Item (b) follows from (a), since $\det(\theta_i(y_j))$ is then a nonzero multiple of $f$ of the same degree. Item (d) holds because $\operatorname{Der}(-\log(D\times\mathbb{C}^k))=\operatorname{Der}(-\log D)\boxtimes\mathcal O\oplus\bigoplus_j\mathcal O\,\partial_{z_j}$. Finally, observe that item (e) is Nakayama's lemma, and item (f) holds because $\operatorname{Der}(-\log f)$ is the kernel of a map of free modules.

label: lem:linear
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:linear}
If $n\ge m+1$ then $\dim\mathcal{L}_{m,n}=m^2+n-1$, and any basis of $\mathcal{L}_{m,n}$ is linearly independent over $R$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: It suffices to show that the fields are independent at a point $p\in U_{m,n}$, i.e.\ that the orbit $G\cdot p$ has dimension $m^2+n-1$. If $(g,t)\cdot p=p$ then $g$ preserves the $n\ge m+1$ lines $\mathbb{C} v_k$, which are in general position, so $g$ is a scalar $\lambda$; then $t_k=\lambda^{-1}$ for all $k$. The stabilizer is therefore one-dimensional.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:psi}
$\psi_{i\to k}\in\operatorname{Der}(-\log f_{m,n})$. It is homogeneous of degree $m\binom{n-2}{m-1}+1$ and $\operatorname{SL}_m$-equivariant. Its multidegree is
\[\Big(\tbinom{n-2}{m-1}(1,\dots,1)\ ,\ \big(\tbinom{n-2}{m-1}-1\big)e_i+\tbinom{n-3}{m-2}\textstyle\sum_{j\ne i,k}e_j+e_k\Big).\]
This multidegree is independent of $i$ if and only if $\binom{n-3}{m-1}=1$, i.e.\ if and only if $n=m+2$ (or $m=1$).

label: thm:terao
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:terao}
If $\mathcal{A}$ is free with exponents $d_1,\dots,d_\ell$, i.e., the degrees of a homogeneous basis of $\operatorname{Der}(-\log\mathcal{A})$, then $\chi_\mathcal{A}(t)=\prod_{i=1}^\ell(t-d_i)$.

label: lem:isotopy
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:isotopy}
Let $B$ be a smooth manifold, $\ell\ge1$, and let $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_N\colon B\to(\mathbb{C}^\ell)^*\setminus\{0\}$ be smooth maps \textup{(}for instance, $B$ a complex manifold and the $\alpha_i$ holomorphic\textup{)}. For $b\in B$ let $\mathcal{A}(b)$ be the central arrangement of the hyperplanes $H_i(b)=\ker\alpha_i(b)\subset\mathbb{C}^\ell$. Assume that the rank function
\[r(S)=\operatorname{rk}\{\alpha_i(b)\mid i\in S\}=\operatorname{codim}\textstyle\bigcap_{i\in S}H_i(b),\qquad S\subset[N],\]
does not depend on $b$. Put
\[\mathcal M=\{(b,x)\in B\times\mathbb{C}^\ell\mid \alpha_i(b)(x)\ne0\ \text{for } 1\le i\le N\}.\]
Then $\mathrm{pr}_1\colon\mathcal M\to B$ is a locally trivial fibration whose fibre over $b$ is $M(\mathcal{A}(b))$. That is, every $b_0\in B$ has an open neighbourhood $V$ with a homeomorphism $\varphi\colon M(\mathcal{A}(b_0))\times V\to\mathcal M\cap(V\times\mathbb{C}^\ell)$ such that $\mathrm{pr}_1\circ\varphi=\mathrm{pr}_2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We use stratifications, Whitney's condition (b) and Whitney stratifications as defined in \cite[Ch.~1, (1.5)--(1.7)]{Dimca}. Complex manifolds are regarded as real ones.

\emph{Step 1: compactifying the fibres.} The projection $\mathcal M\to B$ is not proper. So, as in the proof of \cite[Ch.~1, (4.1)]{Dimca}, we add the hyperplane at infinity. Let $L=\ell+1$ and $P=\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{C}\oplus\mathbb{C}^\ell)\cong\mathbb{P}^\ell$, with homogeneous coordinates $[x_0:x]$. Consider the linear forms on $\mathbb{C}^L$
\[\beta_0=x_0,\qquad \beta_i(b)(x_0,x)=\alpha_i(b)(x)\quad(1\le i\le N).\]
The forms $\beta_1(b),\dots,\beta_N(b)$ do not involve $x_0$. Hence the rank function $\rho(S)=\operatorname{rk}\{\beta_i(b)\mid i\in S\}$, $S\subset\{0,\dots,N\}$, equals $r(S\setminus\{0\})+1$ if $0\in S$ and $r(S)$ otherwise, so it is also independent of $b$. Let $\mathcal E=B\times P$ and $f=\mathrm{pr}_1\colon\mathcal E\to B$. Since $P$ is compact, $f$ is proper. The map $(b,x)\mapsto(b,[1:x])$ is a diffeomorphism of $\mathcal M$ onto the open set
\[\mathcal M'=\{(b,[y])\in\mathcal E\mid \beta_i(b)(y)\ne0\ \text{for } 0\le i\le N\}\]
which is compatible with the projections to $B$, and it identifies $M(\mathcal{A}(b))$ with $\mathcal M'\cap f^{-1}(b)$. It therefore suffices to prove the lemma for $f|_{\mathcal M'}$.

\emph{Step 2: the moving flats.} For $S\subset\{0,\dots,N\}$ let $\widehat X_S(b)=\bigcap_{i\in S}\ker\beta_i(b)\subset\mathbb{C}^L$, a subspace of dimension $L-\rho(S)$, and let
\[\mathcal X_S=\{(b,[y])\in\mathcal E\mid y\in\widehat X_S(b)\},\]
a closed subset of $\mathcal E$. We claim the following. If $s=\rho(S)<L$, then every $b_0\in B$ has an open neighbourhood $V$ and a smooth map $G\colon V\to\operatorname{GL}_L(\mathbb{C})$ such that the diffeomorphism
\[\Theta\colon V\times P\to V\times P,\qquad (b,[w])\mapsto(b,[G(b)w]),\]
maps $V\times\Lambda$ onto $\mathcal X_S\cap(V\times P)$, where $\Lambda=\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{C}^{L-s}\times0)$ is a fixed linear subspace of $P$. To see this, choose $i_1,\dots,i_s\in S$ such that $\beta_{i_1}(b_0),\dots,\beta_{i_s}(b_0)$ are linearly independent. They stay independent on a neighbourhood $V$ of $b_0$. Since $\rho(S)=s$ for every $b$, they span $\langle\beta_i(b)\mid i\in S\rangle$, so $\widehat X_S(b)=\ker A(b)$, where $A(b)$ is the $s\times L$ matrix with rows $\beta_{i_1}(b),\dots,\beta_{i_s}(b)$. After a fixed permutation of the coordinates of $\mathbb{C}^L$ and after shrinking $V$, we can write $A(b)=(A_1(b)\,|\,A_2(b))$ with $A_1(b)\in\operatorname{GL}_s(\mathbb{C})$. Then
\[G(b)=\begin{pmatrix}-A_1(b)^{-1}A_2(b)& I_s\\ I_{L-s}&0\end{pmatrix}\]
satisfies $\det G(b)=\pm1$, and its first $L-s$ columns form a basis of $\ker A(b)$. This proves the claim. Consequently $\mathcal X_S$ is a closed submanifold of $\mathcal E$, and $f|_{\mathcal X_S}$ is a submersion, because in the chart $\Theta$ it becomes the projection $V\times\Lambda\to V$. If $\rho(S)=L$, then $\mathcal X_S=\emptyset$.

\emph{Step 3: the stratification.} For $(b,[y])\in\mathcal E$ let $F(b,[y])=\{i\mid \beta_i(b)(y)=0\}$. Call $F\subset\{0,\dots,N\}$ \emph{closed} if $\rho(F\cup\{i\})>\rho(F)$ for all $i\notin F$. Let $\mathcal F$ be the set of closed $F$ with $\rho(F)<L$. It is finite and independent of $b$. Note that $\rho(F\cup\{i\})=\rho(F)$ if and only if $\widehat X_F(b)\subset\ker\beta_i(b)$. Since $0\ne y\in\widehat X_{F(b,[y])}(b)$, it follows that every $F(b,[y])$ lies in $\mathcal F$. For $F\in\mathcal F$ put
\[\mathcal S_F=\{(b,[y])\in\mathcal E\mid F(b,[y])=F\}=\mathcal X_F\setminus\bigcup_{i\notin F}\mathcal X_{F\cup\{i\}}.\]
The finitely many sets $\mathcal S_F$ partition $\mathcal E$. Each $\mathcal S_F$ is open in $\mathcal X_F$, so by Step~2 it is a submanifold of $\mathcal E$ on which $f$ is a submersion. Discarding empty sets, $\mathcal S=\{\mathcal S_F\}_{F\in\mathcal F}$ is therefore a stratification of $\mathcal E$ in the sense of \cite[Ch.~1, (1.5)]{Dimca}. Since all $\beta_i\ne0$, we have $\emptyset\in\mathcal F$, and the open stratum is $\mathcal S_\emptyset=\mathcal M'$. On each fibre $f^{-1}(b)=P$, $\mathcal S$ induces the stratification of $P$ by the flats of the projective arrangement $\{\mathbb{P}(\ker\beta_i(b))\}_{0\le i\le N}$.

\emph{Step 4: Whitney regularity.} Let $F\ne G$ in $\mathcal F$ and $p=(b_0,[y_0])\in\mathcal S_G\cap\overline{\mathcal S_F}$. As $\mathcal X_F$ is closed, $p\in\mathcal X_F$, i.e.\ $F\subset F(p)=G$, and therefore $\mathcal S_G\subset\mathcal X_G\subset\mathcal X_F$. Choose $V$ and $\Theta$ as in Step~2 for $S=F$ and $b_0$. Condition (1.6) of \cite[Ch.~1]{Dimca} is invariant under diffeomorphisms (see the remark following \cite[Ch.~1, (1.6)]{Dimca}). It therefore suffices to check it for $Y=\Theta^{-1}(\mathcal S_F)$ over $X=\Theta^{-1}(\mathcal S_G)$ at $q=\Theta^{-1}(p)$. Here $Y$ is open in $V\times\Lambda$ and $X\subset V\times\Lambda$. Take a chart of $V$ at $b_0$ and an affine chart of $P$ centred at the second component of $q$; in the latter, $\Lambda$ becomes a linear subspace. In these coordinates we work in an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$ with $q=0$, and $V\times\Lambda$ corresponds to an open subset of a linear subspace $E\subset\mathbb R^m$, with $Y$ open in $E$ and $X\subset E$. Let $x_n\in X$ and $y_n\in Y$ be sequences converging to $0$ as in \cite[Ch.~1, (1.6)]{Dimca}. Then $T_{y_n}Y=E$ for all $n$, so $T=E$. Every secant direction $y_n-x_n$ lies in $E$, so the limit line $l$ lies in $E=T$. This is condition (1.6). (It is the argument behind \cite[Ch.~1, (1.8)(i)]{Dimca}.) Hence $\mathcal S$ is a Whitney stratification of $\mathcal E$ in the sense of \cite[Ch.~1, (1.7)]{Dimca}.

\emph{Step 5: Thom's first isotopy lemma.} The map $f$ is smooth and proper, so $f|_{\overline{\mathcal S_F}}$ is proper for every $F$. By Step~3, $f|_{\mathcal S_F}$ is a submersion. We apply Thom's first isotopy lemma \cite[Ch.~1, Thm.~(3.5)]{Dimca} with $M=A=\mathcal E$ and the Whitney stratification $\mathcal S$. It shows that every $b_0\in B$ has an open neighbourhood $V$ and a homeomorphism $\varphi\colon f^{-1}(b_0)\times V\to f^{-1}(V)$ with $f\circ\varphi=\mathrm{pr}_2$ that preserves the strata, i.e.\ maps $(\mathcal S_F\cap f^{-1}(b_0))\times V$ onto $\mathcal S_F\cap f^{-1}(V)$ for every $F\in\mathcal F$. For $F=\emptyset$ this is a trivialization of $f|_{\mathcal M'}$ over $V$ with fibre $\mathcal M'\cap f^{-1}(b_0)\cong M(\mathcal{A}(b_0))$. By Step~1, this proves the lemma.

The constancy of $r$ was used only in Step~2. Once the moving flats are submanifolds that submerse onto $B$, Whitney regularity is automatic: each stratum is open in a submanifold that contains every stratum meeting its closure.

label: lem:minorsIW
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:minorsIW}
Let $W\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times(n-m)}$ and $N=[I_m\,|\,W]$. For $I=I_1\sqcup(m+I_2)$ with $I_1\subset[m]$ and $I_2\subset[n-m]$ one has
\[\Delta_I(N)=\pm\det W_{[m]\setminus I_1,\,I_2}.\]
The assignment $I\mapsto([m]\setminus I_1,I_2)$ is a bijection between $\binom{[n]}{m}$ and the set of pairs $(P,Q)$, $P\subset[m]$, $Q\subset[n-m]$, $|P|=|Q|$. Thus the maximal minors of $[I_m|W]$ are, up to sign, exactly the minors of $W$ of all sizes, each occurring once, the minor of size $0$ being $\Delta_{[m]}(N)=1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Expand $\det N_I$ along the columns $e_i$, $i\in I_1$: each such column has a single entry $1$, in row $i$. The number of pairs $(P,Q)$ equals $\sum_k\binom mk\binom{n-m}k=\binom nm$.
head: environment

label: prop:slice
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:slice}
Let $\Omega=\{\Delta_{[m]}\ne0\}\subset\mathbb{C}^{m\times n}$. The map
\[\Phi\colon\operatorname{GL}_m\times\mathbb{C}^{m\times(n-m)}\longrightarrow\Omega,\qquad(g,W)\longmapsto g\,[I_m\,|\,W],\]
is an isomorphism of varieties, with inverse
\[M\longmapsto\big(M_{[m]},\,M_{[m]}^{-1}M_{[n]\setminus[m]}\big),\]
and $\Phi^*f_{m,n}=\pm\det(g)^{\binom nm}\mu_{m,n}(W)$. Consequently, $\Phi^{-1}(D_{m,n}\cap\Omega)=\operatorname{GL}_m\times E_{m,n}$ and
\[U_{m,n}\cong\operatorname{GL}_m\times Y_{m,n}.\]
The same holds over $\mathbb{Z}$, hence over every field. For any $I\in\binom{[n]}m$ the analogous statement holds on $\{\Delta_I\ne0\}$, after permuting columns.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Since $\Delta_I(gN)=\det(g)\Delta_I(N)$, this follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:minorsIW}. Moreover $U_{m,n}\subset\Omega$.

label: prop:gale
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Gale duality

title: Proof
body_md: Item (a) follows from the fact that the minors of $W^T$ are the minors of $W$. Then for (b) we observe that the Pl\"ucker coordinates of $\operatorname{rowspace}[I_m|W]$ are the maximal minors of $[I_m|W]$, i.e.\ the minors of $W$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:minorsIW}; a subspace $\Lambda$ with nonzero coordinate $p_{[m]}$ has a unique representative of the form $[I_m|W]$. Finally, item (c) follows from the fact that $\operatorname{rowspace}[I_m|W]^\perp=\operatorname{rowspace}[-W^T|I_{n-m}]$.

label: prop:Y2n
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Y2n}
For $n\ge3$ there are isomorphisms $Y_{n-2,n}\cong Y_{2,n}\cong(\mathbb{C}^*)^{n-1}\times\mathcal{M}_{0}{}_{,n}$, defined over $\mathbb{Z}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $W\in Y_{2,n}$ have columns $(a_j,b_j)^T$, $1\le j\le n-2$. The conditions defining $Y_{2,n}$ are $a_j,b_j\ne0$ and $a_ib_j-a_jb_i=a_ia_j(s_j-s_i)\ne0$, where $s_j=b_j/a_j$. So $W\mapsto\big((a_j)_j,(s_j)_j\big)$ identifies $Y_{2,n}$ with $(\mathbb{C}^*)^{n-2}\times\operatorname{Conf}_{n-2}(\mathbb{C}^*)$. Next, $(s_1,\dots,s_{n-2})\mapsto(s_1;s_2/s_1,\dots,s_{n-2}/s_1)$ identifies $\operatorname{Conf}_{n-2}(\mathbb{C}^*)$ with $\mathbb{C}^*\times\operatorname{Conf}_{n-3}(\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0,1\})=\mathbb{C}^*\times\mathcal{M}_{0}{}_{,n}$. Finally, $Y_{n-2,n}\cong Y_{2,n}$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:gale}(a).

label: thm:complement
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Item (a) follows from Propositions~\ref{prop:slice} and~\ref{prop:gale}. Item (b) follows from the K\"unneth formula and $H^*(\operatorname{GL}_m(\mathbb{C});\mathbb{Z})=H^*(\operatorname{U}(m);\mathbb{Z})=\Lambda_\mathbb{Z}(e_1,e_3,\dots,e_{2m-1})$. Finally, item (c) holds because $\operatorname{GL}_m(\mathbb{C})$ deformation retracts onto $\operatorname{U}(m)$, and $\operatorname{U}(m)\cong\operatorname{SU}(m)\times S^1$ as manifolds via
\[A\longmapsto\big(A\operatorname{diag}(\det A^{-1},1,\dots,1),\ \det A\big).\]

label: rem:Yimtop
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:Yimtop}
For $m=2$, Corollary~\ref{cor:nminus2}(a) is \cite[Thm.~4.1]{Yim}: $(1+t)(1+t^3)(1+t)^{n-1}\prod_{k=2}^{n-2}(1+kt)=(1+t^3)(1+t)^{n-1}\prod_{k=1}^{n-2}(1+kt)$. Item (b) is \cite[Thm.~4.4]{Yim} for the complete graph, since $\operatorname{SU}(2)=S^3$. Item (c) answers \cite[Rem.~4.5]{Yim} in this case. Beyond standard facts about $\mathcal{M}_{0}{}_{,n}$, the proof needs no fibrations or spectral sequences. The fibration obstruction of \cite[Ex.~4.6]{Yim} for $3\times7$ matrices plays no role for the slice, which exists for all $m\times n$; what is not known in general is the topology of $\operatorname{Gr}(m,n)^\circ$.

label: prop:tenplanes
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: (a) If $H_{ij}=H_{kl}$ with $\{i,j\}\ne\{k,l\}$, three of the $P$'s would lie in a plane. (b) Two planes sharing an index meet in $KP_i$, since $P_i,P_j,P_k$ are independent. $H_{ab}\supset KP_i$ forces $i\in\{a,b\}$. Let $\ell=H_{ij}\cap H_{kl}$ with $\{i,j\}\cap\{k,l\}=\emptyset$. If $\ell\subset H_{ab}$ for a third pair, then $\{a,b\}$ meets $\{i,j\}\cup\{k,l\}$ (only one index is left over), say $a=i$ and $b\ne j$. Then $\ell\subset H_{ij}\cap H_{ib}=KP_i$, so $P_i\in H_{kl}$, a contradiction. The same argument shows that $\ell$ is not one of the lines $KP_s$, and that the fifteen lines are distinct. (c) Hence $\sum_{\operatorname{rk} X=2}\mu(X)=5\cdot3+15\cdot1=30$, and $\chi_\mathcal{A}(1)=0$ determines the constant term. (d) If $\mathcal{A}$ were free, Theorem~\ref{thm:terao} would force the roots of $t^2-9t+21$, whose discriminant is $-3$, to be integers.

label: prop:36
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:36}
The projection $\pi\colon U_{3,6}\to U_{3,5}$ forgetting $v_6$ is a locally trivial fibration with fibre $M(\mathcal{A}(v_1,\dots,v_5))$, and
\[\operatorname{Poin}(U_{3,6},t)=(1+t)^6(1+t^3)(1+t^5)(1+2t)(1+3t)(1+9t+21t^2).\]
Equivalently, $\operatorname{Poin}(X(3,6),t)=(1+2t)(1+3t)(1+9t+21t^2)$.

name: $3\times6$ case

title: Proof
body_md:
For $b=(v_1,\dots,v_5)\in U_{3,5}$ and $x\in\mathbb{C}^3$ put $\alpha_{ij}(b)(x)=[v_i,v_j,x]$, $1\le i<j\le5$. The maximal minors of $(v_1,\dots,v_5,x)$ are those of $b$ together with the $\Delta_{ij6}=\alpha_{ij}(b)(x)$. Hence
\[U_{3,6}=\{(b,x)\in U_{3,5}\times\mathbb{C}^3\mid \alpha_{ij}(b)(x)\ne0\ \text{for all } i<j\le5\},\qquad \pi=\mathrm{pr}_1.\]
Since $\ker\alpha_{ij}(b)=\operatorname{span}(v_i,v_j)=H_{ij}$, the vector $v_6$ must avoid exactly the planes $\operatorname{span}(v_i,v_j)$, $i<j\le5$. So $\pi^{-1}(v_1,\dots,v_5)=M(\mathcal{A}(v_1,\dots,v_5))$.

\emph{Local triviality.} We apply Lemma~\ref{lem:isotopy} with $B=U_{3,5}$, $\ell=3$ and the ten forms $\alpha_{ij}$. These are polynomial in $b$, and they are nonzero because $v_i$ and $v_j$ are independent. It remains to show that the rank function
\[r(S)=\operatorname{codim}\textstyle\bigcap_{\{i,j\}\in S}H_{ij},\qquad S\subset\binom{[5]}{2},\]
does not depend on $b$. Any three of $v_1,\dots,v_5$ are linearly independent, so Proposition~\ref{prop:tenplanes} applies with $P_k=v_k$. By part (a), $r(S)=|S|$ if $|S|\le2$. Now let $|S|\ge3$. Then $r(S)\in\{2,3\}$, and $r(S)=2$ if and only if the planes in $S$ contain a common line. This line is then a rank-two flat lying on at least three planes of $\mathcal{A}$. By part (b), this happens if and only if all pairs in $S$ share a common index $i$, the line being $\mathbb{C} v_i$. Thus $r(S)$ depends only on $S$. Lemma~\ref{lem:isotopy} now shows that $\pi$ is a locally trivial fibration with fibre $M(\mathcal{A}(v_1,\dots,v_5))$.

\emph{Cohomology.} The classes $\omega_{ij}=[d\log\Delta_{ij6}]\in H^1(U_{3,6};\mathbb{C})$ restrict on every fibre to the Orlik--Solomon generators $[d\log\alpha_{H_{ij}}]$. Since the Orlik--Solomon algebra is generated in degree one, we can choose monomials $c_1,\dots,c_s$ in the $\omega_{ij}$ whose restrictions form a basis of $H^*(\pi^{-1}(b_0);\mathbb{C})$ for one fixed $b_0$. Consider the set of $b$ for which the restrictions of $c_1,\dots,c_s$ form a basis of $H^*(\pi^{-1}(b);\mathbb{C})$. This set is open and closed. Indeed, let $V$ be a ball over which $\pi$ is trivial. Then the restriction maps $H^*(\pi^{-1}(V))\to H^*(\pi^{-1}(b'))$ are isomorphisms for all $b'\in V$. As $U_{3,5}$ is connected, the $c_k$ restrict to a basis on every fibre. The Leray--Hirsch theorem then gives $\operatorname{Poin}(U_{3,6})=\operatorname{Poin}(U_{3,5})\cdot\operatorname{Poin}(M(\mathcal{A}))$. Now use Corollary~\ref{cor:35top} and Proposition~\ref{prop:tenplanes}(c). The formula for $X(3,6)$ follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:complement} and Example~\ref{ex:Y36}.

body_md: As a check, the coefficient of $t$ is $6+2+3+9=20=\binom63$, the number of components of $D_{3,6}$. Proposition~\ref{prop:36} shows that the Poincar\'e polynomial of $U_{m,n}$ does not in general factor as $\operatorname{Poin}(\operatorname{GL}_m)$ times linear factors over $\mathbb{Q}$. label: prop:localGale
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:localGale}
Let $p\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times n}$ have rank $m$, and choose $I$ with $\Delta_I(p)\ne0$ -- we may assume that after permuting columns $I=[m]$. Write $p=\Phi(g_0,W_0)$ as in Proposition~\ref{prop:slice}, and let $q=[I_{n-m}\,|\,W_0^T]\in\mathbb{C}^{(n-m)\times n}$, a point of rank $n-m$. Then there are isomorphisms of germs
\[(\mathbb{C}^{m\times n},D_{m,n},p)\cong(\mathbb{C}^{m^2},\emptyset,g_0)\times(\mathbb{C}^{m(n-m)},E_{m,n},W_0),\]
\[(\mathbb{C}^{(n-m)\times n},D_{n-m,n},q)\cong(\mathbb{C}^{(n-m)^2},\emptyset,\mathrm{id})\times(\mathbb{C}^{m(n-m)},E_{n-m,n},W_0^T),\]
and $(E_{m,n},W_0)\cong(E_{n-m,n},W_0^T)$ via transposition. In particular $D_{m,n}$ is free at $p$ if and only if $D_{n-m,n}$ is free at $q$. Consequently, $D_{m,n}$ is free at all points of rank $m$ if and only if $D_{n-m,n}$ is free at all points of rank $n-m$.

name: local Gale duality

title: Proof
body_md: Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:slice} to both $D_{m,n}$ and $D_{n-m,n}$, then Proposition~\ref{prop:gale}(a) and Lemma~\ref{lem:standard}(d). Every $W_0\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times(n-m)}$ arises from some point of rank $m$, and every point of rank $n-m$ of $\mathbb{C}^{(n-m)\times n}$ is, after permuting columns, of the form $\Phi(g,W_0^T)$.

label: prop:chart
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:chart}
Let $\Omega'\subset\mathbb{C}^{m\times n}$ be the open set where the leading $(m-1)\times(m-1)$ minor $\det(x_{rk})_{r,k<m}$ is nonzero. Every $M\in\Omega'$ can be written uniquely as
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}B&0\\ r&1\end{pmatrix}\cdot N(Z),\qquad N(Z)=\begin{pmatrix}I_{m-1}&X\\0&z\end{pmatrix},\qquad Z=\begin{pmatrix}X\\ z\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times(n-m+1)},\]
with $B\in\operatorname{GL}_{m-1}$ and $r\in\mathbb{C}^{1\times(m-1)}$. This gives an isomorphism $\Omega'\cong\operatorname{GL}_{m-1}\times\mathbb{C}^{m-1}\times\mathbb{C}^{m\times(n-m+1)}$. Moreover, $\Delta_I(M)=\det(B)\,\Delta_I(N(Z))$, and the maximal minors of $N(Z)$ are, up to sign, exactly the minors of $Z$ \textup{(}of all sizes $\ge1$\textup{)} whose row set contains the last row $m$, each occurring once. Hence
\[D_{m,n}\cap\Omega'\cong\operatorname{GL}_{m-1}\times\mathbb{C}^{m-1}\times E'_{m,n},\qquad E'_{m,n}=V(f'_{m,n}),\quad f'_{m,n}=\prod_{\substack{P\ni m,\ |P|=|Q|}}\det Z_{P,Q}.\]
A point of $\Omega'$ has rank $m-1$ if and only if $z=0$. Every point of $\mathbb{C}^{m\times n}$ of rank $\ge m-1$ can be moved into $\Omega'$ by an element of $S_n\times\operatorname{GL}_m$, which preserves $D_{m,n}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $M=\binom{A}{y}$ with $A\in\mathbb{C}^{(m-1)\times n}$ and $B=A_{[m-1]}$. Then
\[\begin{pmatrix}B&0\\ r&1\end{pmatrix}^{-1}M=\begin{pmatrix}B^{-1}A\\ y-rB^{-1}A\end{pmatrix},\]
and the first $m-1$ entries of the last row vanish exactly when $r=y_{[m-1]}$. This proves existence and uniqueness, and the inverse map is visibly algebraic. For the minors, expand along the identity columns as in Lemma~\ref{lem:minorsIW}: for $I=I_1\sqcup((m-1)+I_2)$ one gets $\pm\det Z_{([m]\setminus I_1),I_2}$, and $[m]\setminus I_1\ni m$. Conversely each pair $(P,Q)$ with $m\in P$, $|P|=|Q|\ge1$ arises from exactly one $I$. The rank statement holds because $\operatorname{rk} N(Z)=m-1+\operatorname{rk} z$. For the last claim, move $m-1$ independent columns to the front and then apply a row operation.

label: ex:chart35
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:chart35}
For $m=3$, $n=5$ we have $Z=\begin{pmatrix}a\\ b\\ c\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{C}^{3\times3}$, rows $a,b,c$ indexed by the columns $3,4,5$, and
\[f'_{3,5}=\prod_{k}c_k\cdot\prod_{j<k}(a_jc_k-a_kc_j)(b_jc_k-b_kc_j)\cdot\det Z,\]
a product of ten forms with $\deg f'_{3,5}=18$ in the $9$ variables $a,b,c$. The point $M_0=(e_1,e_2,0,0,0)$ corresponds to $Z=0$. The seven linear logarithmic fields of $f'_{3,5}$ are spanned by the row and column scalings ($3+3-1=5$ of them) and the two shears $a\mapsto a+\lambda c$ and $b\mapsto b+\lambda c$.

name: the $3\times5$ chart

label: prop:transversal
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:transversal}
In the chart of Example~\ref{ex:chart35}, fix $X=\binom ab$. Then $f'_{3,5}(X,c)$ is the product of the ten linear forms in $c=(c_3,c_4,c_5)$ displayed in Example~\ref{ex:chart35}, and if $X\in Y_{2,5}$ these forms are nonzero and
\[f'_{3,5}(X,c)=\pm\,Q_{\mathcal{A}(P_1,\dots,P_5)}(c),\qquad P_1=a,\ P_2=b,\ P_k=e_k\ (k=3,4,5),\]
where the minor $\Delta_I$ corresponds to the plane $H_{jk}=\operatorname{span}(P_j,P_k)$ with $\{j,k\}=[5]\setminus I$. The vectors $P_1,\dots,P_5$ are in general position if and only if the five columns $e_1,e_2,X_3,X_4,X_5$ of $[I_2\,|\,X]$ are pairwise independent, i.e.\ if and only if $X\in Y_{2,5}$. In that case $(P_1,\dots,P_5)$ is \textup{(}up to signs\textup{)} the Gale transform of the rank-two configuration $(e_1,e_2,X_3,X_4,X_5)$.

title: Proof
body_md: The plane $c_k=0$ contains $e_i,e_j$ with $\{i,j,k\}=\{3,4,5\}$, and corresponds to $\Delta_{12k}$, whose complement is $\{i,j\}$. The plane $b_jc_k-b_kc_j=0$ contains $b=P_2$ and $e_i$, and corresponds to $\Delta_{1jk}$, whose complement is $\{2,i\}$. The plane $a_jc_k-a_kc_j=0$ corresponds in the same way to $\Delta_{2jk}$ and $\{1,i\}$. Finally $\det Z=0$ is the plane $\operatorname{span}(a,b)$, which corresponds to $\Delta_{345}$. General position of the $P$'s means that $a_k,b_k\ne0$ and that all $2\times2$ minors of $X$ are nonzero, i.e.\ $X\in Y_{2,5}$. The Gale transform of $[I_2|X]$ is given by the columns of $[-X^T|I_3]$, see Proposition~\ref{prop:gale}(c).

label: rem:family
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:family}
Non-freeness of the fibres does not formally imply non-freeness of the total space of a non-trivial family. We do not know a general statement of this kind. For $D_{3,5}$ non-freeness is established by computation in Section~\ref{sec:35}. As supporting evidence for a general principle, we checked the family of generic arrangements of five planes in $\mathbb{C}^3$ over its two-dimensional moduli space, $c_1c_2c_3(c_1+c_2+c_3)(c_1+sc_2+uc_3)$ in $\mathbb{C}^5$ with coordinates $(s,u,c)$: it is likewise non-free exactly along $\{c=0\}$.

label: thm:35
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:35}
Let $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{13}$ be a basis of $\mathcal{L}$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=2em]
\item For each $k$, the four fields $\widetilde\psi_{i\to k}$, $i\ne k$, are congruent modulo $R\mathcal{L}$, and none of them lies in $R\mathcal{L}$.
\item $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{13},\Phi_1,\dots,\Phi_5$ is a minimal system of homogeneous generators of $\operatorname{Der}(-\log D_{3,5})$. In particular, the degree-one part of $\operatorname{Der}(-\log D_{3,5})$ is $\mathcal{L}$, and there are no minimal generators in degrees $2,\dots,9$.
\item There are $a_{rj}\in R_{10}$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:syz}
\sum_{k=1}^5x_{rk}\,\Phi_k=\sum_{j=1}^{13}a_{rj}\,\lambda_j\qquad(r=1,2,3),
\end{equation}
and these three relations generate the module of syzygies. Hence the minimal graded free resolution is
\[0\longrightarrow R(-11)^3\xrightarrow{\ \left(\begin{smallmatrix}-A\\ M^T\end{smallmatrix}\right)\ }R(-1)^{13}\oplus R(-10)^5\longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}(-\log D_{3,5})\longrightarrow0,\qquad A=(a_{rj})^T.\]
\item $R\mathcal{L}\cong R(-1)^{13}$ is a free submodule, and $\operatorname{Der}(-\log D_{3,5})/R\mathcal{L}\cong\operatorname{coker}\big(M^T\colon R(-11)^3\to R(-10)^5\big)$.
\item For $p\in\mathbb{C}^{3\times5}$, the stalk $\operatorname{Der}(-\log D_{3,5})_p$ is minimally generated by exactly $18-\operatorname{rk} M(p)$ elements. The non-free locus of $D_{3,5}$ is $\{\operatorname{rk} M\le2\}$, which is irreducible of codimension $3$, and $\operatorname{pd}_R\operatorname{Der}(-\log D_{3,5})=1$.
\item In the $\mathbb{Z}^3\times\mathbb{Z}^5$-grading of Lemma~\ref{lem:psi}, $\Phi_k$ has degree $\big((3,3,3),(2,2,2,2,2)-e_k\big)$, and the syzygy \eqref{eq:syz} has degree $\big((3,3,3)+e_r,(2,2,2,2,2)\big)$.
\end{enumerate}

title: Corollary

\label{cor:nonfreelocus}
The non-free locus of $D_{3,5}$ is exactly the determinantal variety $\{\operatorname{rk} M\le2\}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By Corollary~\ref{cor:fullrankfree}, $D_{3,5}$ is free at points of rank $3$. Let $p$ have rank $2$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:chart}, some $\sigma\in S_5\times\operatorname{GL}_3$ moves $p$ into $\Omega'$, where it corresponds to a point with $c=0$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:chart} and Lemma~\ref{lem:standard}(d), $D_{3,5}$ is free at $p$ if and only if $E'_{3,5}$ is free at the corresponding point, and it is not by Proposition~\ref{prop:certificate}(b). Points of rank $\le1$ lie in the closure of the rank-two locus, and the non-free locus is closed.

title: Remark
body_md: If $D_{3,5}$ were free, Lemma~\ref{lem:standard}(b) would force a basis consisting of the $13$ linear fields and two fields of degrees $d_1+d_2=30-13=17$. This is impossible by Theorem~\ref{thm:35}(2), since the next minimal generators occur in degree $10$. The resolution in (3) is consistent with the determinant of $\operatorname{Der}(-\log f)$ being $R(-\deg f)$: $13\cdot1+5\cdot10-3\cdot11=30$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Let $\rho\colon\{\operatorname{rk} M=3\}\to\operatorname{Gr}(3,5)$ send $M$ to its row space $\Lambda$. On the open set $\{\operatorname{rk} M=3\}$, the module $\operatorname{coker}(M^T)$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:35}(4) is the pull-back of the tautological quotient bundle $\mathbb{C}^5/\Lambda$, a vector bundle of rank $2$. So, over $\{\operatorname{rk} M=3\}$ and modulo the vector fields tangent to the $\operatorname{GL}_3\times(\mathbb{C}^*)^5$-orbits, the logarithmic vector fields of $D_{3,5}$ are sections of $\rho^*(\mathbb{C}^5/\Lambda)(-10)$. On all of $\mathbb{C}^{3\times5}$, the sheaf $\operatorname{coker}(M^T)$ is locally free exactly where $\operatorname{rk} M=3$.

In general, $\operatorname{rank}\operatorname{Der}(-\log D_{m,n})-\dim\mathcal{L}_{m,n}=mn-m^2-n+1=(m-1)(n-m-1)$, the dimension of the moduli space of $n$ points in general position in $\mathbb{P}^{m-1}$. For $2\times5$ this quotient is free of rank $2$ ($\operatorname{Der}(-\log D_{2,5})\cong R(-1)^8\oplus R(-6)^2$); for $3\times5$ it is the non-free rank-two sheaf above.

title: Remark
body_md: All five $\Phi_k$ have row degree $(3,3,3)$. Hence the degree-$10$ part of $\operatorname{Der}/R\mathcal{L}$ is a sum of copies of the character $\det^3$ of $\operatorname{GL}_3$, and its generators can be chosen $\operatorname{SL}_3$-equivariant, as they are. By the first fundamental theorem of invariant theory, every $\operatorname{SL}_3$-equivariant polynomial vector field on $\mathbb{C}^{3\times5}$ has the form $M\mapsto M\cdot C(M)$, with $C$ a $5\times5$ matrix of polynomials in the Pl\"ucker coordinates $\Delta_I$. For $\psi_{i\to k}$ one has $C=c_{i\to k}E_{ki}$, the simplest possible choice in the weight spaces of Theorem~\ref{thm:35}(6).

label: prop:Hk
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Hk}
In the chart of Proposition~\ref{prop:chart}, fix $X\in Y_{m-1,n}\subset\mathbb{C}^{(m-1)\times(n-m+1)}$, i.e.\ assume that the columns of $[I_{m-1}|X]$ are in general position. Then $f'_{m,n}(X,z)$ is a product of $\binom nm$ nonzero linear forms in $z\in\mathbb{C}^{n-m+1}$. They define the arrangement $\mathcal H_{n-m}(P)$ of the hyperplanes spanned by the $(n-m)$-element subsets of the $n$ vectors
\[P=(X_1,\dots,X_{m-1},e_1,\dots,e_{n-m+1})\]
in $\mathbb{C}^{n-m+1}$, where $X_p$ are the rows of $X$. Up to signs, $P$ is the Gale transform of the $n$ columns of $[I_{m-1}|X]$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The minor $\det Z_{P',Q}$ with $m\in P'$ is linear in $z$. It vanishes at $z=e_j$ for $j\notin Q$ (the last row of $Z_{P',Q}$ is then zero) and at $z=X_p$ for $p\in P'\setminus\{m\}$ (two equal rows). These $(n-m+1-|Q|)+(|P'|-1)=n-m$ vectors are independent, since $P$ is in general position (Gale duality preserves general position), so they span the zero set. Conversely every $(n-m)$-subset of $P$ arises from exactly one pair $(P',Q)$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),leftmargin=2em]
\item $m=n-1$: $\mathcal H_1(P)$ consists of $n$ lines through the origin in $\mathbb{C}^2$, which is always free. This is consistent with $D_{n-1,n}$ being a linear free divisor.
\item $m=2$: $\mathcal H_{n-2}(P)$, for $P=(X_1,e_1,\dots,e_{n-1})$ in $\mathbb{C}^{n-1}$, is linearly equivalent (take $X_1=(1,\dots,1)$) to the essential braid arrangement $\{z_i=0\}\cup\{z_i=z_j\}$ in $\mathbb{C}^{n-1}$, of type $A_{n-1}$, which is free with exponents $1,\dots,n-1$. This is consistent with Yim's theorem.
\item $m=n-2$: $\mathcal H_2(P)$ is the arrangement of the $\binom n2$ planes spanned by pairs of $n$ generic vectors in $\mathbb{C}^3$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:pairs}).
\item $3\times6$: $\mathcal H_3(P)$ consists of $20$ hyperplanes in $\mathbb{C}^4$ spanned by triples of $6$ generic vectors. A direct computation of the intersection lattice for a random integral configuration gives
\[\chi(t)=(t-1)(t^3-19t^2+126t-300),\]
whose cubic factor is monotone and has a single real root in $(7,8)$. So this arrangement is not free, by Theorem~\ref{thm:terao}.
\end{enumerate}

label: prop:pairs
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:pairs}
Let $n\ge4$ and let $P_1,\dots,P_n\in\mathbb{C}^3$ be generic. Then the arrangement of the $N=\binom n2$ planes $\operatorname{span}(P_i,P_j)$ has characteristic polynomial
\[\chi(t)=(t-1)\big(t^2-(N-1)t+b_n\big),\qquad b_n=n(n-2)+3\tbinom n4-N+1.\]
The discriminant of the quadratic factor is $-\tfrac14(n-2)(n-3)(n^2-5n+2)$, which is negative for $n\ge5$. Hence the arrangement is free for $n=4$ (it is the braid arrangement, $\chi=(t-1)(t-2)(t-3)$) and not free for $n\ge5$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: For generic points, the rank-two flats are the $n$ lines $\mathbb{C} P_i$, each in $n-1$ planes, and the $\frac12\binom n2\binom{n-2}2=3\binom n4$ lines $\operatorname{span}(P_i,P_j)\cap\operatorname{span}(P_k,P_l)$ with $\{i,j\}\cap\{k,l\}=\emptyset$, each in exactly two planes; compare Proposition~\ref{prop:tenplanes}, where for $n=5$ general position suffices. Therefore $\sum_{\operatorname{rk} X=2}\mu(X)=n(n-2)+3\binom n4$, and $\chi(1)=0$ gives the constant term. The discriminant is a direct computation. For $n=5,\dots,8$ the lattice was also computed for random integral configurations; the quadratic factors are $t^2-9t+21$, $t^2-14t+55$, $t^2-20t+120$ and $t^2-27t+231$.

label: conj
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conj}
For $1\le m<n$, the divisor $D_{m,n}$ is free if and only if $m\le2$ or $n=m+1$. Moreover, for $3\le m\le n-2$ the non-free locus contains all matrices of rank at most $m-1$; for $m=n-2$ it is exactly $\{\operatorname{rk} M\le n-3\}$.
